drhp.business: Bombay Dyeing operates through three distinct business divisions - Polyester, Realty and Retail - each tailored to meet distinct market demands. The Polyester Staple Fibre (PSF) division is a B2B manufacturer supplying domestic and international customers in the non-woven and spinning industries, where PSF is a critical input material; the Company continues to operate as one of the five producers of PSF in the country. risks.note: Significant new capacity additions across the sector over the last nine years have created a substantial domestic surplus; the prevailing excess capacity has been the primary driver of lower margins across the sector and has led to aggressive price undercutting, while the Company operates as a stand-alone polyester manufacturer against a single fully vertically integrated market leader.
risks.risk: Structural domestic PSF oversupply and price undercutting

risks.note: The Company's profitability remains sensitive to the cost of raw materials and energy, both heavily dependent on global crude oil prices; the fiscal year was characterized by extreme volatility in crude, which directly influenced the cost of PTA and MEG, and domestic availability of these raw materials remained tight, necessitating continued reliance on imports to sustain optimum operating rates.
risks.risk: Crude oil and petrochemical input cost volatility

risks.note: Major input costs are denominated in US Dollars, so fluctuations in the Indian Rupee/US$ exchange rate present a continuous risk to margins.
risks.risk: Rupee / US Dollar exchange rate exposure

risks.note: Man-Made Fibres are taxed at 18%, significantly higher than cotton, inflating production costs and discouraging fresh capital investment; Indian PSF prices also remain substantially higher than those in China, and tariff issues in the USA disrupted the textile industry through 2025-2026.
risks.risk: Adverse tax and trade policy - inverted GST and import price parity

risks.note: The West Asia conflict involving Iran and the USA and other global hotspots may disrupt trade flows, logistics networks and supply chains, influence crude and transportation costs, and pressure construction inputs such as crude oil derivatives and steel; any escalation or delay in resolution remains a primary area of concern for the business environment.

Tariff measures in certain international markets have hurt export competitiveness for textile manufacturers, so surplus export-intended inventory may be redirected into the domestic market at discounted prices, causing dumping and heightened price competition, on top of intense competition from domestic brands, private labels, international décor retailers and unorganized low-price participants.
risks.risk: Import dumping and price competition in home textiles

risks.note: Demand for PSF is closely linked to the supply and pricing of the domestic and global cotton crop, and fluctuations in cotton and other input prices lead to pricing uncertainty and margin pressure across the home textile business; rising logistics and distribution costs further affect retail profitability.
risks.risk: Cotton and raw material price volatility in the retail business

risks.note: Elevated construction input costs challenge margins particularly on fixed-price contracts and further commodity escalation could impact project viability; regulatory approval delays and evolving compliance requirements may affect project timelines, dependence on external financing and liquidity conditions could influence project rollout, and sustained price increases may erode affordability in the mid-income segment leading to demand moderation.
risks.risk: Real estate execution, regulatory and affordability risk
